analysis.one_liner: Bars most employer health plans from imposing lifetime benefit caps below $5 million.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the floor on lifetime health insurance caps never got a vote, dying in committee after being referred on the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop employer health plans and insurers from putting a dollar cap lower than $5 million—and later $10 million—on total lifetime benefits for a worker or family. It covers plans under ERISA and the Public Health Service Act, but exempts employers with fewer than 20 employees. No further action was taken after its introduction and referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families with expensive chronic or catastrophic illnesses, whose care can exhaust low lifetime caps and leave them uninsured mid-illness. The roughly 130 million Americans with employer-sponsored coverage benefit from the security of knowing their benefits cannot run out at a low ceiling.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans and their insurers from imposing an aggregate lifetime limit below $5 million in the first three plan years after enactment, and below $10 million thereafter.
Applies the floor to both ERISA plans and group coverage regulated under the Public Health Service Act, closing the main routes group coverage takes.
Covers an individual or other coverage unit, so family coverage could not be capped at a low total for the household.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and health insurers, who would face higher expected claims costs for enrollees with very high cumulative medical bills; in practice much of this would be passed through to premiums.

drawbacks.text: Higher lifetime floors raise insurers' and employers' expected costs, and plans commonly offset mandates through higher premiums, which are borne by employers and workers through wage and premium effects.
The bill exempts small employers with fewer than 20 employees, so employees of most small businesses—a large share of the private workforce—would not get the protection.
The mandate applies only to group plans, so it does nothing for people buying individual coverage or uninsured.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real and targeted at a genuine hardship—plans could exhaust benefits mid-illness—but it is narrow: small employers are exempt and the individual market is untouched. The cost, higher premiums, is diffuse; the benefit, avoiding catastrophic loss of coverage, is concentrated on the people who most need it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Labor and Human Resources Committee in July 1997, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Senate introduced the bill on July 31, 1997, and the same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
No further action appears in the full action history; the bill never received a hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote in the 105th Congress.
The Congress ended January 3, 1999, so the bill died in committee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and health insurers benefit from the status quo, in which plans may continue imposing low lifetime aggregate caps without a federal floor. The 12 cosponsoring senators' proposal did not advance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers keeping status quo

for.name: Sen. James M. Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: Twelve Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, including Democratic leader Tom Daschle.

against.name: Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no recorded action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party agenda-setters in the 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the Senate floor during the 105th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and all 12 cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill never advanced far enough to produce a partisan vote.

industries.note: The bill sets a floor on lifetime benefit limits, raising expected claims for plans covering people with very expensive conditions. Insurers' cost-containment interest runs against patients whose care would exceed the caps.
Employers with 20 or more employees would bear higher expected benefit costs and possible premium increases. Small employers are exempt.
